transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-16
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Jade (Redwood SE), Aisha (NovaHealth CTO), Ben (Lead ML Eng), Carla (Security)

[00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick agenda — 1) run through JSON / structured output mode, 2) show function/tool calling flows, 3) guardrails and security, and 4) Q&A + next steps. sound good?

[00:28] Aisha (NovaHealth): yep that works. our main goals today are to validate the structured output for our claims routing microservice and to understand end-to-end security — we have PHI concerns so private deployment options matter.

[00:55] Jade (Redwood SE): great. i'll start with a quick demo in the console: JSON mode. so this is Redwood's structured output flag — you can pass a JSON schema and the model will try to conform to it. i'll paste a sample schema for a claim_summary object. note — in practice we layer schema validation client-side too.

[01:22] Ben (NovaHealth): quick question: how strict is the schema? like, will it always return valid JSON or do we still need to parse/handle errors?

[01:38] Jade: good q. we surface two modes — 'constrained' which enforces the schema during generation with a strict parser + deterministic fallback, and 'soft' which biases generation but accepts partials. in our demo i'll show constrained mode and the function-calling guardrail that triggers a re-call or structured repair if the payload is malformed. transcription note: i said "constrain-ed" earlier which the recorder picked up oddly.

[02:15] Samir: also worth calling out — Redwood Optimize can recommend the schema granularity and batching settings to balance latency vs token cost; small, flatter schemas tend to be cheaper.

[02:43] [Jade shares console screen — live code snippet]

[03:05] Jade: here's a sample prompt + schema. i send the prompt to the hosted endpoint in JSON mode, and the runtime returns a JSON payload. you can also wire that to a function call. for example, if claim_summary.action == 'escalate' we call the escalate_ticket tool.

[03:40] Ben (NovaHealth): tool calling — is that webhook-based? we need to call internal microservices that live in our VPC.

[03:55] Jade: yes, two options: 1) use function calling where the model returns a structured call intent and Redwood will surface it as a call activity for your app to execute, or 2) configure an internal tool runner in Private deployments where the runtime can invoke your private endpoints directly (this requires VPC peering / private network). small transcription glitch: i said "tool runner" but it sounded like "toll runner" in part.

[04:30] Carla (Security): on private invocation — curious about credentials; how do we provision KMS secrets and maintain audit logs?

[04:45] Jade: we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS), and for Private we support HSM-backed key stores. audit logs are shipped to your logging bucket or centralized SIEM; every function call and model response can be traced with token-level latency and cost metadata in the Console.

[05:12] Samir: i'll drop the SOC 2 and iso summary into the chat after this call. we also have an architecture note for PHI in Private deployments.

[05:28] Aisha: cool. another big concern — hallucinations. we need determinism for billing decisions; if the model invents fields in the JSON that's a showstopper.

[05:44] Jade: understood. two practical guardrails we use: schema enforcement + output validators, and a hybrid approach where model suggests fields but a lightweight deterministic function (checksum-based or rules engine) validates before downstream action. Redwood can automatically retry with higher temperature constraints or fall back to a smaller exact-match model when schema compliance fails.

[06:20] Ben: do you have performance numbers? our SLA for routing is sub-200ms 95th p90 for simple claim decisions.

[06:35] Jade: p90/p95 depends heavily on model and batch settings. for hosted low-latency models we have p95s in the 80-130ms range for ~128 token responses. on Dedicated you can get single-digit token latencies with optimized kernels and continuous batching tuned for your sequence length. Optimize will recommend quantization/ batching configs based on your workload trace. note: i fumbled a brand name — said "dedicate" instead of Dedicated earlier.

[07:10] Samir: also routing policy — if latency spikes we can failover to a cheaper hosted variant or degrade to cached KV responses for known prefixes. that keeps the system up for core routing decisions.

[07:45] Aisha: what's the expected engineering effort for Private? we have an internal compliance window of 6 weeks to stand up a PoC if we commit.

[08:00] Jade: typical Private PoC is 3-6 weeks depending on networking approvals. key tasks: VPC peering/networking, KMS integration, sample data ingestion, and running our benchmark harness. we'll provide a deployment checklist.

[08:28] Ben: on the schema itself — can we test stricter types like enums and nested lists? our claim items are arrays of procedure codes.

[08:45] Jade: yes, schemas support nested arrays, enums, and required properties. we demoed an array earlier — the model returned an out-of-order element once and we used the repair flow to reorder and revalidate. small transcription error: "re-validate" got glued to "repairflow" in the notes.

[09:10] [Demo: function calling flow]

[09:30] Jade: watch the function call: model returns a call with arguments that match the schema, Redwood maps that to a function stub and we can execute a mock webhook. if the function execution fails, Redwood can capture the error and send the user a structured error object so downstream consumers are stable.

[10:02] Carla: is there an audit trail for function inputs/outputs? we need to keep a tamper-evident log for audits.

[10:18] Jade: yes — every request, function intent, and tool execution is logged and can be exported. for high-security customers we recommend Private with tamper-evident storage options.

[10:40] Samir: quick note on cost: structured output can reduce token usage because you avoid verbose natural language; but complex nested schemas sometimes increase tokens. Optimize can simulate cost estimates for your prompt+schema.

[11:05] Ben: can Optimize suggest simplified schemas? we want a balance: enough fields to make decisions but not too many to blow up cost.

[11:20] Jade: yes — Optimize will analyze historical traces and recommend schema alterations, batching, and quantization. it can also recommend model variants (float16 vs 4-bit quantized) per-route.

[11:45] Aisha: about data retention — we can't keep PHI in hosted logs for more than 30 days. what's Redwood policy?

[12:00] Samir: hosted default retention is 90 days, but Enterprise/Private tiers can customize retention; Private can be configured to keep zero logs or ship logs to your S3/GCS with lifecycle policies. we'll include retention options in the security doc.

[12:28] Ben: are there pre-built connectors to our PagerDuty / ticketing system for escalations?

[12:40] Jade: we have templates for Slack, PagerDuty, and webhooks. function results can be forwarded to those integrations via the Console or via your own runner in Private.

[13:05] Aisha: any limitations around PHI being used for training? we cannot allow any of our data to be used for model training.

[13:22] Samir: we do not use customer data for training in Hosted or Private; customers can opt-out and that's captured in contract. we'll include language in the security pack.

[13:40] [Demo: Console — showing route configs and per-token cost breakdown]

[14:05] Jade: here i create a route: /claims/summary -> model_x_small with JSON schema and a fallback model. you can set a routing policy: latency-first or cost-first. i toggle to latency-first to show the fallback behavior.

[14:35] Ben: if a schema repair triggers multiple retries, how's cost accounted? do we get consolidated billing per logical request?

[14:50] Samir: billing is per API call + tokens. we provide aggregated metrics per logical request in the Console so you can see retries, token counts, and costs. Optimize will flag high-retry routes.

[15:20] Carla: legal — procurement wants specific indemnity language for PHI. who at Redwood handles that?

[15:35] Samir: i'll loop in our legal/enterprise team when we move to contract. for the PoC we'll provide a draft MSA and data processing addendum.

[16:00] [Longer pause / side conversation about onboarding credits]

[17:10] Jade: quick follow-up: for the demo i also showed a "repair tool" pattern where the model returns a partial JSON and a secondary function fills in missing required fields deterministically. works well for strict compliance flows.

[18:00] Ben: can that repair be deterministic and idempotent? we can't have double-charges or duplicate ticket creation.

[18:15] Jade: yes — implement idempotency keys at the function level; Redwood will surface the idempotency key and you can gate downstream actions.
